rashi:a1.1: According to the one who says, etc.: it is a dispute in Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 57b): there is one who says a tereifa gives birth, and there is one who says it does not give birth.
rashi:a2.1: Both this and that cause: one cannot place the dispute in whether a fetus is the thigh of its mother except where it became pregnant and afterward became a tereifa, for there, according to the one who says it is its mother’s thigh, the tereifa condition occurred in its own body. But where it became a tereifa and afterward became pregnant, one cannot say it is its mother’s thigh, since it has a permitted side in it [its father]; rather, they disagree about “both this and that cause.”
tosafot:a1.1:
According to the one who says a tereifa cannot give birth, you find it where it became pregnant and afterward became a tereifa, and they disagree about whether a fetus is the thigh of its mother: this is puzzling. For it said above [30b] that where it became pregnant and afterward was the object of bestiality, everyone agrees it is prohibited, since it and its offspring were both objects of bestiality; and here it says that according to the one who says a tereifa cannot give birth, you find it where it became pregnant and afterward became a tereifa, and the Rabbis hold it is permitted because it is not its mother’s thigh. And we hold in Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 58a) that a tereifa does not give birth; if so, let us say Rava is not in accordance with the Rabbis.
One can say: certainly with a tereifa condition, which depends on vitality and health, since we see the offspring alive and healthy, we have no reason to say that the offspring became a tereifa together with its mother, and no reason to disqualify it on account of the tereifa disqualification. But with bestiality and goring, it is certainly like its mother’s thigh.
Yet there is a slight difficulty: if so, the mishna speaks of different cases, for with the offspring of an animal that was the object of bestiality one must say that they were objects of bestiality and afterward became pregnant, and with the offspring of a tereifa one must say that they became pregnant and afterward became tereifot, since the conclusion in Elu Tereifot is that a tereifa does not give birth. One can say: since with a tereifa a fetus is relevant in only one way, it does not count as speaking of different cases, for the mishna comes only to tell you all the permitted offspring of all the animals prohibited for the altar. With the object of bestiality, where there are two possibilities and it is permitted in only one, the mishna counts it for the sake of that permitted possibility; and with the tereifa, where there is only one possibility, it counts that permitted possibility.
gershom:a1.1: Rabbi Eliezer holds that a fetus is the thigh of its mother: just as its mother is prohibited, since it is a tereifa, so too the offspring.
rashi:a4.1: A chick: that hatched from the egg of a tereifa dove, that it is prohibited to be sacrificed. The offspring in an animal’s womb is not attached to its body but hangs in open space, and it forms and grows by itself; but an egg, as long as it is not complete, is attached to the cluster [of eggs inside the bird] and grows and is completed from the hen’s body. Another version: [the animal’s offspring] grows in the open air after it is born, and goes on growing, so the main part of its growth is not from its mother; but an egg grows from the hen’s body, and the matter proves itself, since after it has come out it does not grow. That is why the Rabbis concede. The wording of the Yerushalmi.
tosafot:a4.1: That grows from open space: that is, the offspring in an animal’s womb is not attached to its body but hangs in open space, and it forms and grows by itself; but an egg is joined to the cluster. Another version: it grows in the open air after it is born, and goes on growing, so the main part of its growth does not come from its mother; but an egg grows from the hen’s body, and the matter proves itself, since after it is laid it does not grow. Rashi explained both versions.
gershom:a2.1: The Sages concede to Rabbi Eliezer with regard to a chick that emerged from a tereifa’s egg, that it is prohibited to be eaten: whether according to the first version or according to the latter version, for there, in tractate Ḥullin, there are two versions. With a chick that emerged from a tereifa’s egg, according to the first version it is not comparable to the offspring of a tereifa: there it has a permitted element in it, and “both this and that cause” is permitted, while the chick has no permitted element in it, for we established there that the tereifa’s egg is from the first batch, which separated from its mother’s body; therefore it is prohibited. And according to the latter version, an egg too is the thigh of its mother, since it is from its mother’s body, coming from the cluster of eggs that is attached to her body; that is, it grows in prohibition from her own body.
gershom:a3.1: Rather, with the offspring of an animal, which grows from open space: which grows after it is born, in the open air of the world, and grows in permission. But a tereifa’s egg does not grow after it is laid; all its growth is inside the hen, in prohibition, and so even the Rabbis concede that it is prohibited.
rashi:a5.1: Rava said to Rav Huna, etc.: [his support holds] on the first version, according to the one who says a tereifa gives birth; on the latter version, according to the one who says a tereifa does not give birth, [it speaks of] the first batch of eggs, which were already in the cluster when the hen became a tereifa.
rashi:a5.2: A full ladle: in tractate Nazir (50b) its measure is explained.
rashi:a5.3: That comes from a living person: and afterward he died.
rashi:a5.4: Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure: since it is his body; and the Rabbis disagree with him only, etc. [Another version, and this is the main one:] Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure even during his lifetime, since a limb from a living person imparts impurity by contact, by carrying and in a tent, like a limb from a corpse, as in HaOr VeHarotev (Ḥullin 128b). But with a chick, even Rabbi Eliezer concedes that it may be sacrificed, since it is a different body, and this body was never in the womb of the tereifa.
tosafot:a5.1:
A full ladle of worms that come from a living person who afterward died, Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure, since it is his body, and the Rabbis disagree with him only, etc.: Rashi further explained, “And it seems to me that Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure even during his lifetime, since a limb from a living person imparts impurity by contact, by carrying and in a tent,” as in HaOr VeHarotev (Ḥullin 128b).
This is puzzling: in tractate Nazir, chapter Kohen Gadol (51b), it asks: if he rotted while alive and then died, what is the law? But what is its question? Rabbi Eliezer deems it impure: on the first explanation [when he died], and on the second explanation even if he did not die, all the more so if he died. One can say that it asks according to the Rabbis: perhaps the Rabbis deem pure only worms, which are mere secretion and not of the person’s body but a creature of their own, but with rot they concede. And in the Gemara there, to resolve the question, it brings the passage I cited from HaOr VeHarotev (128b): Rabbi Yehoshua said: No; if you said so of the dead, which has a majority, a quarter and rot, will you say so of the living, which has no majority, quarter or rot? And the Ri says that Rabbi Yehoshua is the Rabbis here, who hold that a living person has no worms [that impart impurity], for according to Rabbi Eliezer, since he has worms, all the more so he has rot.
And the Ri, brother of my teacher, asked: here it teaches “a full ladle of worms,” while in the Mishna (Oholot 2:2) we learned: an olive-bulk of worms, whether living or dead, imparts impurity, the words of Rabbi Eliezer, and the Sages deem it pure. And it seems to my teacher that [the ladle] is specifically when it separated from a living person, and then the measure is a full ladle. But that is not so, for in any case, what is the measure of a ladle doing here?
gershom:a4.1: A full ladle of worms: worms that come from a living person, and afterward he died. Rabbi Eliezer deems that full ladle of worms impure, in a tent and by contact.
gershom:a5.1: And the Sages deem it pure: since it separated during his lifetime and is like mere dust, and it does not impart impurity, since it is not of his body.
gershom:a6.1: But with a chick that emerged: since the egg is from the hen’s body, as we said, even the Rabbis concede that it is a full offspring and like her body, and prohibited. Abaye said to him: On the contrary, etc.
tosafot:a6.1: But a person is called a worm, etc.; but an egg, when does it grow? When it rots, and when it rots it is mere dust: this is puzzling: why did he need to state the first reason? One can say it is only to add strength to the matter: even if a person were not called a worm, worms are in any case not comparable to the egg of a chick.
rashi:a7.1: After it rots: after the egg has rotted, this chick emerges from it; and when it rotted its prohibition lapsed, since it became mere dust. Therefore this one, which emerges from it afterward, is permitted.
gershom:a7.1: Another version: but a chick, when does it develop from the egg, that is, when is it formed in the egg? After it rots, when it is entirely permitted. At that time it is formed, and the egg is mere dust, since it is not fit for eating, and it became permitted. Therefore he concedes that it is permitted.
gershom:a8.1: And furthermore, it is explicitly taught: Rabbi Eliezer concedes to the Sages that it is permitted to be eaten.
rashi:a8.1: So too, that it is prohibited?: But it was said above that only an animal set aside [for idolatry] is prohibited through being fed vetches, but one not set aside is not.
gershom:a9.1: If so, if one fed it vetches of idolatry: this is not speaking of one who handed it over to the idolatrous priests; rather, he himself fed it, not for the sake of any idolatry, and it was fattened from them. So too, would it be prohibited?
rashi:a9.1: Warm milk every morning: all its days.
rashi:a9.2: Since it can survive: on that morning’s milk for twenty-four hours without any other food, and when the twenty-four hours were up it suckled again. Therefore all of its growth is from her [the tereifa], even if it ate other things in between.
tosafot:a9.1: That suckled warm milk: and the same is true of vetches of idolatry: if it ate them all its days, so that the main part of its growth was from them, it is prohibited; and on a cursory reading, even for ordinary use.
gershom:a10.1: Rather, Rabbi Ḥanina Terita taught: what are we dealing with here, in the words of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus? Where it suckled a tereifa’s warm milk from morning to morning. Since by virtue of that milk it can survive without food for twenty-four hours, so that it needs no other food, it grows entirely from the tereifa and is prohibited. But with vetches of idolatry, it cannot survive on them for twenty-four hours and needs other food, and so it is permitted.
gershom:a11.1: One may not redeem them: since they are prohibited for eating and are fit only for dogs, and one does not redeem for dogs, because it degrades consecrated items; rather, they should die and be buried.
rashi:a10.1: “Notwithstanding … after all the desire of your soul … flesh”: we establish this verse as referring to disqualified consecrated animals, in the Sifrei of the house of Rav.
gershom:a12.1: As the Sages taught: “Notwithstanding, after all the desire of your soul”: it is speaking of disqualified consecrated animals.
gershom:a13.1: “You may slaughter,” but not shearing: you are not permitted to shear them.
gershom:a14.1: “And eat”: you, and not your dog.
gershom:a15.1: “And eat flesh,” but not milk: for it is prohibited to milk consecrated animals, since that is labor.
rashi:a11.1: Some say: “You may slaughter and eat flesh,” you have no permission to eat them except from the time of slaughter: this excludes milk and shearing, which are a benefit from it while alive. But one may redeem consecrated animals to feed them to dogs, since “and eat” is not left over for him to expound “and not your dogs.” And from this exposition it is implied that for your dogs it is fine, for this is what it means: you may not eat before slaughter, that is, you may not benefit from it while it is alive; but your dogs, which comes after death, is fine even without slaughter. And whether one may redeem consecrated animals to feed them to dogs is a dispute of two tanna’im, and so we establish it in Shechitat Ḥullin (102a).
gershom:a16.1: From here, that one may not redeem, etc. Some say: “You may slaughter and eat” comes entirely to teach that you have permission with them only from the time of slaughter onward, when it is fit to be eaten, but before then it is prohibited for shearing and for labor. And since he does not expound “and eat” to exclude, evidently he holds that one may redeem consecrated animals, etc.
gershom:a17.1: We will return to you, Kol HaAsurin.
rashi:a14.1: Mishna: items consecrated for Temple maintenance: we exclude them at the end of the first chapter (above, Temurah 13a) from rendering a substitute.
gershom:a18.1: There are elements that apply to items consecrated for the altar, etc.: items consecrated for Temple maintenance do not render a substitute, since they are not called an “offering”; and furthermore, they are consecrated only for their value. And their offspring and their milk are prohibited after their redemption, as we established there in tractate Bekhorot, in the second chapter: where it became pregnant before its redemption and gave birth after its redemption.
rashi:a14.2: Piggul, notar and impure, etc.: these are written with regard to peace offerings, and in the first chapter of Yevamot (7a) it explains: peace offerings were included among all the consecrated items, so why were they singled out? To compare to them and tell you: just as peace offerings are distinctive in being consecrated for the altar, so too all items consecrated for the altar.
tosafot:a13.1: Mishna: There are elements that apply to items consecrated for the altar … [liability] due to piggul: as it says at the end of chapter Beit Shammai in Zevaḥim (46a): why are there three [statements of] karet with peace offerings? One for the general rule and one for the particular, that is, to apply the principle of something that was included in the general rule and left it (the text adds: “that were distant”): just as peace offerings are consecrated for the altar, so too all items consecrated for the altar. And notar is derived from piggul through the verbal analogy “iniquity”–“iniquity,” and impurity from notar through the verbal analogy “profanation”–“profanation.”
rashi:b1.1: Their offspring and their milk: we derived [the milk] above, at the end of Kol HaAsurin: “flesh,” and not milk. Their offspring: it is explained in the second chapter of Bekhorot (14a) as where it became pregnant before its redemption and gave birth after its redemption, for which there is no remedy: to sacrifice them is impossible, since they come by virtue of a rejected sanctity; to redeem them, [the mother’s redemption] was not strong enough to take hold of them. But if it became pregnant after its redemption, they are the offspring of a gazelle and a deer, and permitted. And with items consecrated for Temple maintenance, even where it became pregnant before their redemption they are permitted, since they were consecrated only for their value, and their sanctity is not so severe.
tosafot:b1.1: Their offspring and their milk are prohibited after their redemption: in Bekhorot (14a) it establishes this as where it became pregnant before their redemption and gave birth after their redemption. For if it became pregnant and gave birth before their redemption, it said above in chapter Elu Kodashim (Temurah 17b): “if” comes to include the offspring of blemished animals, either to be sacrificed, according to the one who holds so, or to graze, according to the one who holds so. And if it became pregnant after their redemption, they are called the offspring of a deer and a gazelle. Rather, it is certainly speaking of where it became pregnant before their redemption and gave birth after their redemption, for their mothers’ redemption does not help them, since they are unblemished in their mothers’ womb; even if a blemish befalls them once they are born they are not permitted, as is taught there, since [the redemption] is not strong enough to take hold of them. And they are sacred: since it became pregnant before their redemption, they became sacred at once, according to the one who says they are sacred in their mothers’ womb; and even according to the one who says [they become sacred] at their birth, when at the time of their birth their mothers are non-sacred, in any case sanctity took hold of them at their birth.
gershom:b1.1: And one does not give from them to the craftsmen as the wages of those who build the Temple.
rashi:b2.1: Takes effect on everything: even on stones and on wood.
rashi:b2.2: And one is liable for misuse of their by-products: the Gemara explains the reason.
gershom:b15.1: And there is no benefit for the priests [our mishna reads “for the owner”] from them: in consecration for Temple maintenance.
gershom:b2.1: Whose is this mishna? It is Rabbi Yehuda, who says that even offspring renders a substitute.
gershom:b3.1: When the mishna teaches that items consecrated for the altar render a substitute, it refers to the principal offering: this excludes a substitute and offspring, which are not the principal offering, and so the mishna can be established even according to the Rabbis.
tosafot:b7.1: But items consecrated for Temple maintenance are given; from where are these matters derived?: this is puzzling: what else would we do with them, if not give them to craftsmen as their wages for strengthening the Temple’s upkeep? And my teacher HaRaMaR says: it would enter our mind that it is permitted to buy with them only wood and stones, which are needs of the building and whose sanctity remains on them; but to give them to craftsmen as their wages, and thereby take them out to non-sacred status, is prohibited, and money would instead be donated separately to pay the craftsmen. That is why the verse was needed: from the very funds that were consecrated, one gives to the craftsmen.
rashi:b8.1: Gemara: The Master said: Unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance: and even an animal is included.
rashi:b8.2: Who is the tanna: who holds that even animals, if one consecrated them without specification and did not say “for the altar,” we say he consecrated them for Temple maintenance? Not Rabbi Yehoshua.
rashi:b9.1: And their money shall be allocated with the rest of the property, etc.: Rabbi Eliezer holds that unspecified consecrations are for Temple maintenance, even an animal; yet anything fit for the altar, when one redeems it from the treasurer, one redeems it only for the altar, since it never leaves the altar’s hold, as is taught below in this chapter: one who dedicates unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, when they are redeemed, they are redeemed only for the altar.
tosafot:b9.1: Males shall be sold for the needs of burnt offerings: because we hold below (Temurah 33b) that one who dedicates unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, they do not leave the altar’s hold. And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that the males are sacrificed as burnt offerings, since a person does not abandon sanctity for the altar and consecrate with sanctity of value. Evidently, according to Rabbi Yehoshua unspecified consecrations are not for Temple maintenance.
gershom:b4.1: Rabbi Eliezer says: Males shall be sold for the needs of burnt offerings and females shall be sold for the needs of peace offerings: because it is taught: one who consecrates unblemished animals for Temple maintenance, when they are redeemed, they are redeemed only for the altar, for anything fit for the altar never leaves the altar’s hold. And their money shall go to Temple maintenance. From Rabbi Eliezer’s saying “they shall be sold and their money shall be allocated,” evidently he holds that an unspecified consecration is for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b10.1: Rabbi Yehoshua says, etc.: evidently, with something fit for the altar, its unspecified sanctity is for the altar.
gershom:b5.1: Rabbi Yehoshua says: The males themselves shall be sacrificed as burnt offerings, for the altar, since items consecrated for Temple maintenance are entirely for God, and a burnt offering is entirely for God; therefore the males themselves shall be sacrificed as burnt offerings. But the females, which are not entirely burned, shall be sold, and he shall bring burnt offerings with their money, for Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a person divides his vow.
gershom:b6.1: One who consecrates his property: that is, whatever among it is fit for the altar, he does not abandon sanctity for the altar and consecrate it for Temple maintenance. Evidently the animal is for the altar and the rest of the property for Temple maintenance.
rashi:b11.1: And it disagrees with Rav Adda: this, that he established the mishna in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer, disagrees with Rav Adda, who said that according to Rabbi Eliezer too, one who consecrates an animal without specification consecrates it for the altar; and here this is the reason: because a person does not divide his vow, half for one sanctity and half for another.
tosafot:b11.1: And it disagrees with Rav Adda bar Ahava: who said that even according to Rabbi Eliezer unspecified consecrations are not for Temple maintenance; and here the reason is because a person does not divide his vow, and since there are females here, which must be sold [the males are sold too].
gershom:b7.1: And Rabbi Eliezer holds that a person does not divide his vow: one who consecrates without specification, it is all for Temple maintenance; for just as the females he could not consecrate as burnt offerings, so too the males he did not consecrate as burnt offerings, since a person does not divide his vow. Therefore both these and those are sold, and their money goes to Temple maintenance. And this, that Rabbi Eliezer says a person does not divide his vow, so that he consecrated the males only for their value, is what disagrees with Rav Adda bar Ahava, for Rav Adda bar Ahava said, etc.
gershom:b8.1: That even Rabbi Eliezer concedes that yes, they themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings; rather, where they disagree is with a herd that has, etc.
rashi:b13.1: A person divides his vow: the males as burnt offerings and the females for the value of burnt offerings. One cannot say [the females are] peace offerings, to be sacrificed without redemption, for since he would eat them, he would come to misuse: presumably he did not say they are peace offerings, and since he consecrated everything, he may not benefit from them.
gershom:b9.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that a person divides: the males themselves are sacrificed as burnt offerings, and the females are sold and he brings burnt offerings with their money.
rashi:b14.1: Only animals: all his animals. Even Rabbi Eliezer concedes that, although there are females, since all the animals are fit for the altar we say his unspecified consecration is for the altar; the males are sacrificed as burnt offerings, and the females are sold for the needs of peace offerings and their money goes to burnt offerings, since one can say that the entire vow is for the altar.
rashi:b17.1: But according to the first version: where Rav Adda said that with a herd half males and half females, Rabbi Eliezer says a person does not divide his vow, half to sacrifice the body itself and half to sacrifice its value; and even where there is no other property, and one could say the entire vow is for the altar, Rabbi Eliezer disagrees. Why, then, does he teach “their money shall be allocated with the rest of the property for Temple maintenance”? Sometimes there is no other property at all!
rashi:b18.1: Shavings and fallen leaves: if one consecrated a tree for Temple maintenance, there is misuse with the shavings, if he planed it, and there is misuse with its fallen leaves, the leaves that fall in the winter and serve him as fertilizer.
tosafot:b18.1: To add shavings and fallen leaves: and it is speaking of one who consecrates the beam; for with treasurers who bought wood, it says in Me’ila at the end of chapter Vlad Ḥatat (Me’ila 14a) that one is not liable for misuse of the shavings or the fallen leaves. And now one must explain: what does “which is not so with items consecrated for the altar” mean? How do shavings and fallen leaves apply to items consecrated for the altar? One can say: for example, one who consecrates two logs of wood for the arrangement [on the altar].
gershom:b10.1: Consecration for Temple maintenance takes effect on everything. Ravina said: to add shavings and fallen leaves: if one consecrated wood for Temple maintenance, the consecration takes effect also on the shavings, the sawdust that falls when one cuts it, and on the fallen leaves, the leaves that fell from it. This is not so with items consecrated for the altar, as it says in tractate Me’ila, chapter Vlad Ḥatat (14a): treasurers who bought wood for the arrangement [on the altar]: one is liable for misuse of the wood but not of the shavings and fallen leaves.
gershom:b16.1: Even with shavings and fallen leaves of Temple maintenance, for one is liable for misuse of them.
tosafot:b19.1: And one is liable for misuse of their by-products; to add what?: the wording is difficult, for it should have said “to exclude what?”
rashi:b19.1: Milk of consecrated animals: the milk of consecrated animals. With items consecrated for the altar it mentions turtledoves, [which are fit] for the altar; and with items consecrated for Temple maintenance it mentions a chicken and not turtledoves, since it speaks of the usual way of things, for one does not usually consecrate for Temple maintenance something fit for the altar.
gershom:b11.1: And one is liable for misuse of by-products: to include the milk of an animal consecrated for Temple maintenance and the eggs of turtledoves consecrated for Temple maintenance, that one is liable for misuse of those consecrated by-products too, as we learned: milk, etc.
rashi:b20.1: Its female donkey: this is a novelty, for although it is non-kosher, the sanctity of Temple maintenance takes effect on it as on something pure.
gershom:b12.1: In what case is this said? With items consecrated for the altar, since these by-products are not fit for the altar.
gershom:b13.1: But with items consecrated for Temple maintenance: even with a donkey consecrated for Temple maintenance, one is liable for misuse of its milk, although it is not fit for eating.
rashi:b21.1: By-products that are fit for the altar: such as the offspring of consecrated animals.
tosafot:b21.1:
And even according to the one who says one is liable for misuse of items consecrated for the altar, that applies to by-products fit for the altar: Rashi explained, such as offspring. But it seems to me that offspring are certainly not sacred by reason of being by-products but by reason of what is written, “which you have” (above, Temurah 17b): these are the offspring. And it is further difficult, for I have not found any tanna who holds that one is liable for misuse of by-products of the altar: with by-products of items consecrated for Temple maintenance I have found tanna’im who disagree, in Me’ila (13a), but with items consecrated for the altar, everyone agrees one is not liable for misuse.
And my teacher HaRaMaR says: perhaps this is Ze’iri, who said in Me’ila, chapter Vlad Ḥatat (Me’ila 12b): one who lets blood from a consecrated animal is liable for misuse of it. And Rav Hamnuna objected to him: But didn’t we learn: milk of consecrated animals and eggs of chickens [our baraita reads “pigeons”]: one may not benefit from them, but one is not liable for misuse? Since he objects to him from by-products, evidently he considers blood a by-product. That is why it says “even according to the one who says one is liable for misuse of by-products,” and this is its meaning: even according to the one who says there is misuse with blood, that applies to blood that is fit to be sprinkled; but by-products such as milk of consecrated animals and turtledoves’ eggs, no.
gershom:b14.1: And even according to the one who says one is liable for misuse of by-products of the altar: here, with these by-products, such as milk and turtledoves’ eggs, which are not fit for the altar, one is not liable for misuse.
